claims.text: A refractory HEA based on Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and V can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature fusion plasma-facing components.
The proposed refractory HEA would be an improved structural material compared with tungsten.
A stable single-phase microstructure can be engineered in the proposed low-activation refractory HEA.
The proposed HEA is expected to have enhanced irradiation resistance.
The proposed HEA is expected to have lower neutron-induced activation than tungsten.
A more uniform distribution of irradiation-induced defects would reduce the formation of deleterious helium bubbles.
The proposed refractory HEA would be synthesized in equiatomic or near-equiatomic proportions as a single-phase solid solution.
Fusion plasma-facing components must operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K while exposed to deuterium, tritium, helium, and neutrons.
Fusion plasma-facing components experience very high particle fluxes under long-duration operation.
The proposed single-phase microstructure would remain stable under high-temperature, high-flux irradiation.
A stable single-phase microstructure would mitigate the accumulation of irradiation-induced defects.
A stable single-phase microstructure would mitigate helium-bubble accumulation.
The multiprincipal-element design distributes irradiation damage over multiple lattice sites.
Distributing irradiation damage over multiple lattice sites reduces local embrittlement and helium-bubble formation.
Selecting constituent elements with low neutron cross sections minimizes activation and limits the production of long-lived radioactive species.
Under fusion-relevant conditions, the proposed HEA would retain better mechanical integrity than tungsten.
Under fusion-relevant conditions, the proposed HEA would show less helium-induced blistering than tungsten.
Under fusion-relevant conditions, the proposed HEA would exhibit lower induced radioactivity than tungsten.
Tungsten has low fracture toughness and undergoes brittle transgranular and intergranular failure.
Tungsten develops deuterium- and helium-induced blistering, pits, holes, and bubbles under plasma exposure at relevant temperatures.
